name: Underpromotion
summary: Promoting to a knight with 1.e8=N+ forks the black king and queen, winning the queen where a new queen would do nothing.
intro: Underpromotion is the deliberate choice to promote a pawn to a rook, bishop, or knight instead of the all-powerful queen. It is rare because the queen is usually best, but in specific positions a lesser piece does something the queen cannot: deliver a knight's fork, avoid a stalemate, or dodge an immediate loss. Knowing when to underpromote separates the sharp from the merely strong.
boardCaption: White to move; the e7-pawn is one step from queening, but 1.e8=N+ underpromotes to a knight, forking the king and queen.

sections.heading: The Idea
paragraphs: When a pawn reaches the last rank, a new queen is nearly always the strongest choice. Yet the queen moves like a rook and bishop, never like a knight. In positions where only a knight's leap achieves the goal, promoting to a queen would waste the moment. Underpromotion to a knight fills exactly that gap, adding a check or fork no queen could give.

The other classic reason to underpromote is stalemate avoidance: a brand-new queen can accidentally leave the enemy king with no legal move and no check, drawing a won game. Choosing a rook instead can keep the win alive. Underpromotion is a specialist's tool, reached for only when the standard queen fails to do the job.

sections.heading: The Line
paragraphs: A new queen on e8 would achieve nothing concrete here, but the knight promotion is decisive. White plays 1.e8=N+, and the newly minted knight on e8 checks the king on g7 while simultaneously attacking the queen on c7. It is a fork born the instant the pawn transforms, striking two targets at once.

Black must attend to the check first, stepping aside with 1...Kg8. That frees the knight to complete its errand: 2.Nxc7 captures the black queen. The pawn that seemed destined to become a queen instead became a knight, and in doing so won the enemy's most valuable piece. The lesser promotion proved the greater move.

sections.heading: How To Spot It
paragraphs: When a pawn is about to promote, pause before automatically choosing the queen. Ask whether a knight promotion would give check or fork, especially if the enemy king and a heavy piece stand a knight's move apart. The moment of promotion is your chance to place a knight on a square it could never otherwise reach with tempo.

Also watch for stalemate traps in winning endgames: if a new queen would leave the opponent with no move, consider a rook or a check-giving underpromotion instead. These situations are uncommon, so train your eye to notice the geometry of a knight fork or the danger of stalemate exactly when the pawn touches the eighth rank.

keyIdeas: Underpromotion chooses a rook, bishop, or knight over the usual queen.
A knight promotion can give a check or fork no queen can.
Here 1.e8=N+ forks the king on g7 and queen on c7.
After 1...Kg8 the knight wins the queen with 2.Nxc7.
Underpromotion also saves won games from accidental stalemate.
Pause at every promotion to check whether a knight does more.
